chapter: Later life, World's Fair and Ellington
title: Meeting and marrying Elizabeth Hefner
summary: He describes his wife, her family and how she first played piano with him at Brew's.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives

blocks.x: Now, you wanted to talk about -- finish talking about the family, Now, we've got a new family, When did you meet Elizabeth,
Elizabeth? I met Elizabeth -- well, I met her before I married her, so that was four and a half years ago,
Does she teach under her maiden name or her --
Now she teaches under --
Elizabeth Hall?
Hefner Hall, yes.
Elizabeth Hefner Hall.
Yeah, and she's the chairman of the Art Department at Southern Connecticut State College and teaches classes also, professor.
Uh-huh, and has had shows.
Yes, we've had shows at Long Island University, and I have one we've invited you to December 11th.
(Laughter.)
And she has a son, Peter Hefner, in Chicago that works for Minnesota Mining, and a daughter, Laura, who's 17 -- 16, still attending school in New Haven.
She's got a daughter and a granddaughter the same age almost.
Yes. Yes. They hang out together sometimes.
That's great.

But the rest of her family is so great, this is what I meant by after you learn how to play and what happens around you, how you play. She has a very distinguished family. Don Turner's a professor at Harvard in law. And Bard Turner is an inventor that invented some part of the gadget that worked for the space program.
Uh-huh. Now, these are her --
Brothers.
-- brothers.
And --
Oh, Turner is her maiden name.
Yeah, Turner's her maiden name, and another brother in Wisconsin who's a dentist.
And you met her because she's a pianist? Is that --
No, as a matter of fact, we got married -- and she told me she played the piano, but I never heard her. We never practiced together.
Oh, because you mentioned to me about her coming up on the stand at Brewis.
But we had never practiced together. That was the first time we played together --
I see.
-- when she came to Brew's.
You were playing at Brew's on 34th Street.
Yes. Yes. Yeah, it was -- and the pianist that was hired didn't show, and I coaxed her up on the stand, and she did real well, well enough to be hired again.
(Laughter.)
But when you met her, you didn't know she was a pianist.
I guess we talked about it. I just knew her as an artist. I didn't know she was a professor either.
(Laughter.)
Well, would you say that music brought you together then?
Right. Yes, it certainly did.
